name: The Right to an Explanation
title: The Right to an Explanation
answer: The right to an explanation is the idea that a person affected by an automated decision should be able to learn why that decision was made. It sits inside emerging legal frameworks rather than inside computer science, and it draws on data protection law, administrative law and consumer protection. The subject covers who can ask, what counts as a sufficient answer, and when a general description of a system is enough. It applies most often to decisions about credit, employment, insurance, benefits and similar determinations.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: The right to an explanation is the idea that a person affected by an automated decision should be able to learn why that decision was made. It sits inside emerging legal frameworks rather than inside computer science, and it draws on data protection law, administrative law and consumer protection. The subject covers who can ask, what counts as a sufficient answer, and when a general description of a system is enough. It applies most often to decisions about credit, employment, insurance, benefits and similar determinations.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The right runs on the ordinary machinery of decision systems: training data, model weights, feature sets, thresholds and the logs that record what a system did on a given day. In practice an explanation is assembled from model documentation, input records, version histories and audit trails, not from the model itself. That means the quality of the right depends on record keeping that was designed before anyone asked the question. Where records are thin, the explanation becomes a reconstruction rather than a report.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Work in this area is done by lawyers, compliance staff and technical teams reading the same decision from different angles. A typical request is answered by tracing the inputs, the model version and the rule or score that produced the outcome, then writing that trace in language the affected person can follow. Regulators and courts have accepted several forms, from a short statement of the main factors to a fuller account of the logic involved. The hard part is usually not the law but the gap between what a system can output and what a person can understand.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The right sits alongside other duties: notice, data access, human review and, in some sectors, impact assessment. It is enforced through data protection authorities, sector regulators and private claims, and it overlaps with the broader wave of AI litigation and rulemaking that this site tracks. Provenance matters here, because an explanation is only as good as the record of which data and which model version produced the decision. Teams that keep versioned logs, documented feature choices and clear ownership of each system find these requests far easier to answer.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect the right to be defined less by statute and more by decisions in individual cases, as regulators and courts work through what a sufficient explanation looks like. Standardised model documentation and decision logs are likely to become the practical currency of compliance. The open questions are how much detail is owed, how trade secrets are handled, and whether an explanation must be understandable to the person affected rather than merely accurate. As automated decisions spread into more areas, the right will keep being tested against systems that were never built to explain themselves.
